p34.title: Cinema ticket price
p34.statement:
Read a person's age (an integer) and print the ticket price **in tomans**, by this rule:

- under 6 years: `0`
- from 6 to 17 years (both included): `50000`
- from 18 to 64 years: `90000`
- 65 years and above: `40000`

Print only the price number.
hints: The prices: under 6 years `0`, 6 to 17 years `50000`, 18 to 64 years `90000` and from 65 years up `40000`.
The boundaries matter: ages 6 and 17 are in the 50000 range, 18 is in the 90000 range and 65 is in the 40000 range.

solutions.name: Method 1: an elif chain
steps: We read the age.
If it is less than 6, the price is zero.
With `elif` we check the next ranges; the last case is with `else`.
explain: In an `elif` chain each range is checked only when the earlier ranges did not match. So `age < 18` means an age from 6 to 17 (because under 6 was already separated).
Each age has only one price, because only one of the blocks runs.

solutions.name: Method 2: change the price little by little
steps: We set the price to `0`.
If the age is at least 6, we make the price `50000`.
If it is at least 18, we make the price `90000`; and if it is at least 65, `40000`.
At the end we print the price.
explain: This method writes the `if`s one after another. The order matters: each later `if` that is true changes the earlier price. For the age 70 all three conditions are true, but the last change is `40000`.
Both methods give the same answer. Method 1 is good for simpler boundaries and method 2 is good for understanding how a value changes.

p35.title: Triangle type from three sides
p35.statement:
Read three positive lengths `a`, `b` and `c`, each on its own line.

If all three are equal, print `equilateral`; if exactly two are equal, print `isosceles`; otherwise print `scalene`.
hints: First check the case of all three being equal.
Then check with `or` whether two of the sides are equal.
p35.guideTitle: Triangle type from three sides — nested conditions and elif
mistakes: Checking the two-equal case before the three-equal case: an equilateral triangle has two equal sides too.

solutions.name: Method 1: elif with checking equality
steps: We read the three sides.
If all three are equal, it is `equilateral`.
If two are equal, it is `isosceles`.
Otherwise `scalene`.
explain: The order of the conditions matters: first the case of all three sides equal is checked, because every equilateral triangle satisfies the two-equal condition too. If the order is changed, the answer becomes wrong.
`or` is true when at least one of the three pairs is equal. With `elif` we separate that two-equal case.

solutions.name: Method 2: nested conditions
steps: If `a` and `b` are equal, we check whether `c` is equal too.
If `a` and `b` are not equal, we check which pair is equal.
If no pair was equal, `scalene`.
explain: This method starts with a nested condition to show that one problem can be solved with two structures. The result is what the first method gives.
In the branch `if a == b`, if `c` is equal too it is equilateral; otherwise exactly two sides are equal and it is isosceles.

p82.title: Name of the weekday with elif
p82.statement:
Read a number `n`. If `n` is from 1 to 7, print the name of the day in English:

- 1 ← `Saturday`
- 2 ← `Sunday`
- 3 ← `Monday`
- 4 ← `Tuesday`
- 5 ← `Wednesday`
- 6 ← `Thursday`
- 7 ← `Friday`

For any other number print the word `invalid`. **elif** is needed for this.
hints: Write each case as a separate `elif`; the order of the conditions does not matter, but each number satisfies only one condition.
Put the cases outside 1 to 7 in the `else`.
p82.guideTitle: Name of the weekday with elif
mistakes: Writing `if` for all the cases: all the conditions are checked and more than one print may happen.

solutions.name: Method 1: an elif chain with print
steps: We read the number.
For each number from 1 to 7 we have an `elif` that prints the name of the day.
If none matched, we print `invalid`.
explain: The `if / elif / else` chain runs the branch of the first true condition and skips the rest. Each number falls into only one branch.
Zero and numbers greater than 7 have no branch and reach `else`; so `invalid` is printed.

solutions.name: Method 2: choosing the name in a variable and one print
steps: We take a variable `name` for the name of the day.
With the `elif` chain we decide the value of `name`.
At the end we print `name`.
explain: This method only decides the value of `name` in the branches and writes `print` once at the end. The structure of the program becomes simpler and each case is defined in only one place.
Each number is compared with `elif` exactly once, so the tests for zero and for numbers greater than 7 also get the name `invalid`.

p10.title: Sum with for
p10.statement:
The input is in this form:

- first line: the number `n` (how many numbers follow)
- then exactly `n` integers; each on its own line

Print the sum of those `n` numbers.

**Only with `for`** (no `while`). Do not use the call `sum(...)`; calculate the sum yourself in the loop. The name of the sum variable is free.
hints: The first input is the count of the following numbers; read it separately and in the `for` loop take that many numbers.
Set the sum variable to zero before the loop and add each number to it inside the loop; `sum` is forbidden.
p10.guideTitle: Sum with for — accumulating in a variable

solutions.name: Method 1: calculate the sum at the moment of reading
steps: We read the count `n`.
We set the variable `total` to zero.
We read a number `n` times and add each one to `total`.
At the end we print `total`.
explain: If we write `total = total + x`, it means take the previous value, add `x` to it and put it back into `total`. We repeat this `n` times.
Starting from zero matters, because if we do not create `total`, Python does not know the empty variable and gives an error.

solutions.name: Method 2: first put all the numbers in a list
steps: We read the count and make an empty list.
With `append` we add the numbers to the list.
With a loop over the list we calculate the sum and print it.
explain: In this method we have two loops: the first collects the numbers and the second calculates the sum. For a simple problem like this, method 1 is shorter.
The second method is useful when we want to use the numbers again later, for example to find the largest or the average.

p11.title: Multiplication table of a number
p11.statement:
Read the number `k` (`1 ≤ k ≤ 9`) and print its multiplication table from 1 to 10; each row exactly in this form:

`k x i = result`

Format notes:

- the letter `x` is a lowercase English letter (not the Persian multiplication sign)
- there is exactly one space between the parts
- example for `k=2` and `i=3`: `2 x 3 = 6`

**Only with `for`** (no `while`).
hints: The loop runs over `i` from 1 to 10; `range(1, 11)` gives this range.
`print` with several arguments puts a space between them; the letter `x` must be English and lowercase.
p11.guideTitle: Multiplication table of a number — for and formatted printing

solutions.name: Method 1: print with several arguments
steps: We read the number `k`.
With `for i in range(1, 11)` we give `i` the values 1 to 10.
Each time, with `print` we print the form `k x i = result`.
explain: `range(1, 11)` gives the numbers 1 to 10. On each run of the loop, `k * i` calculates the product.
We put the letter `x` inside quotes so that the English letter `x` is printed, not the multiplication sign. `print` puts the spaces itself.

solutions.name: Method 2: building each row with + and str
steps: We read the number `k`.
On each run of the loop we build a complete string (with `+`).
We print the string.
explain: `str` turns a number into text so that we can join it with `+` to other texts. If we put a number directly next to a text with `+`, Python gives an error.
The result of both methods is the same. Method 2 gives full control over the spaces, but it is longer.

p12.title: Food countdown
p12.statement:
Read a positive integer `m` (`m ≥ 1`). From `m` down to `1`, for each value `X` print this line:

`Time remaining: X minutes`

Then print exactly this line:

`Your food is ready!`

Write the English text letter by letter as in the example. Even when `X` is 1, write the same word `minutes` (not `minute`).

**Only with `for`.**
hints: `range(m, 0, -1)` gives the numbers from `m` to `1` in decreasing order.
Even for `1` write the word `minutes`; print the text of the last line separately after the loop.
p12.guideTitle: Food countdown — for with a negative step

solutions.name: Method 1: range with a negative step
steps: We read the number `m`.
`range(m, 0, -1)` gives the numbers `m` down to `1` in descending order.
For each number we print the line `Time remaining`.
At the end we print the line `Your food is ready!`.
explain: `range(m, 0, -1)` starts at `m`, subtracts one at a time and stops before `0`; so the last number is `1`.
Write the word `minutes` for all the numbers, even `1`, as it is asked.

solutions.name: Method 2: counting up and calculating the remainder
steps: `range(1, m + 1)` gives the numbers 1 to `m`.
We calculate the remainder with `m - i + 1`; when `i` is 1, the remainder is `m`.
We print the same text as before.
explain: In this method the loop counter goes up, so we must calculate the remainder ourselves. The formula `m - i + 1` always gets us to the right number.
This method gets the mind used to calculating with a counter; the answer of both methods is the same.

p18.title: Only the positive numbers
p18.statement:
The first line is the number `n`, and then `n` integers (each on its own line) come.

Print only the **positive** numbers (greater than zero), **each on its own line**. Zero and negative numbers must not be printed.
hints: For each number write an `if` that prints only the positive ones.
The number zero is not positive.
p18.guideTitle: Only the positive numbers — a loop over the input and if
mistakes: Writing `x >= 0`: zero is printed too, when it must not be.

solutions.name: Method 1: for and the positive condition
steps: We read the count of numbers `n`.
With `for` we read the next number `n` times.
If the number is greater than zero, we print it.
explain: The first line of the input tells the count of numbers and then each number comes on its own line. So the `for` loop runs exactly `n` times and in each round we read one line.
Zero and negative numbers are rejected with the condition `x > 0`. We must read the input in that same round, not all of it before the loop.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with a counter
steps: We read the count of numbers and start the counter from zero.
As long as the counter is less than `n`, we read the next number.
If it is positive we print it, and we increase the counter by one.
explain: This method does the same job with `while`. The counter `i` shows the number of numbers read, and the condition `i < n` makes the loop run exactly `n` times.
Increasing the counter at the end of the round matters; if we forget it, the loop stays true forever and the program becomes endless.

p36.title: Sum of the even numbers
p36.statement:
Read the natural number `n` (`n ≥ 1`).

Print the sum of all the **even** numbers between 1 and `n` (including `n` if it is even).

Example: for `n = 10` the answer is `2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30`.
hints: `range(2, n + 1, 2)` gives only the even numbers from 2 to `n`.
Start the sum from zero; if you take all the numbers, find the even ones with `%`.
p36.guideTitle: Sum of the evens — for with a step

solutions.name: Method 1: range with step 2
steps: We read the number `n` and set `total` to zero.
`range(2, n + 1, 2)` gives the numbers 2, 4, 6 ... up to `n`.
We add each one to `total`.
explain: The third number of `range` is the step. With a step of 2 we start from 2 and take only the even numbers, so there is no need to check for evenness.
If `n` is `1`, the range `range(2, 2, 2)` is empty and the answer becomes zero, which is correct.

solutions.name: Method 2: take all and separate the evens
steps: We take all the numbers from 1 to `n`.
For each number we check the remainder of dividing by 2.
If it is zero, we add it to the sum.
explain: This method looks harder, but it shows the idea of being even clearly: an even number means `% 2` is zero.
Both methods give the same answer; method 1 is faster because it does not see the odd numbers at all.

p37.title: Product of the numbers
p37.statement:
First read the count `n` (a natural number) and then `n` integers, each on its own line.

Print the product of all these numbers.

Example: `2 3 4` → `24`
hints: Start the product from `1`, because multiplying by `1` does not change the number.
If one of the numbers is `0`, the final result becomes `0`; there is no need for a special case, just multiply all of them.
p37.guideTitle: Product — for and accumulating in the result

solutions.name: Method 1: do the multiplication at the moment of reading
steps: We read the count `n`.
We set the result to `1`.
We read a number `n` times and multiply each one into the result.
We print the final result.
explain: Starting from `1` matters: if we start from `0`, every multiplication stays zero. If we start from `1`, the first number becomes exactly that number.
`product = product * x` means multiply the previous value by `x` and put it back into `product`. This is repeated `n` times.

solutions.name: Method 2: first put everything in a list
steps: We save the numbers in a list.
With a `for` over the list we build the product.
explain: This method has two steps: first collecting and then calculating. When we need to use the numbers again later, this method is more useful.
The output of both methods is the same.

p38.title: Are all the numbers positive?
p38.statement:
The first line is `n` (`n ≥ 1`), and then `n` integers (each on its own line) come.

If **all** the numbers are positive, print `all positive`, otherwise print `not all positive`.
hints: Make a variable that is true at first; make it false when you see any non-positive number.
At the end check that same variable.
p38.guideTitle: Are all the numbers positive? — a flag and counting
mistakes: Printing inside the loop: we must announce the result after all the numbers.

solutions.name: Method 1: a flag (a true/false variable)
steps: We assume everything is positive; that is, we set the variable `all_pos` to `True`.
We read each number; if it is zero or negative, we make `all_pos` `False`.
At the end we print the answer based on `all_pos`.
explain: A flag is a "true/false" variable that holds the state of the whole input. With one non-positive number, the flag becomes `False` forever, because nowhere do we make it `True` again.
Since we read all the numbers, the program reads the input completely and no mismatch with the input happens. This matters, because if we finished earlier, the remaining inputs would not be read.

solutions.name: Method 2: counting the positive numbers
steps: We set a counter for the positive numbers.
We count each positive number.
If the counter equals `n`, all are positive.
explain: Instead of a flag, this method counts the number of positive numbers. If this count equals `n`, it means there was no non-positive number.
Both methods give the same answer; a flag is more common for questions of this kind.
